summary: The note explains how the lasting rise of remote work after 2020 is reshaping real estate by decentralizing cities. Demand is moving to suburbs and secondary cities, commercial office vacancies are rising, and developers and investors are adapting. It also covers technology's role, sustainability benefits, and expert views that cities are changing rather than dying.
one_line: Remote work is driving urban decentralization, pushing real estate demand, development and investment from city centers toward suburbs and secondary cities.
key_facts: A FlexJob Solutions study found 58% of the workforce engages in some form of remote work, with 36% working fully from home.
High-rise offices in cities like New York and San Francisco have reported vacancy rates as high as 20% since late 2023.
Michael Peters, CEO of Urban Commercial Realty, said in October 2023 that landlords and investors are converting commercial spaces into residential units, shared workspaces, or community centers.
The U.S. Census Bureau's November 2023 report found suburbs and secondary cities grew at three times the rate of major metropolises in the last year.
Thomas Keller said on December 10, 2023 that central urban rents are stagnating or decreasing while peripheral areas have a bullish market, an inversion of the historic norm.
In January 2024 the National Association of Home Builders reported a 15% increase in permits for single-family homes in suburban areas, versus 3% for urban apartments.
On February 16, 2024, tech analyst Laura Smith said high-speed internet is now a basic utility and a deciding factor in real estate choices.
Dr. Rajiv Chaudhary said in a March 2024 panel that 'Cities are not dying, but they are changing,' pointing to more distributed economic prosperity.
Dr. Melanie Turner's study released April 5, 2024 found remote workers report higher satisfaction and lower stress, and reduced commutes cut carbon emissions.
Venture capitalist James Donovan said at a May 2024 investment summit that real estate is now about 'adaptability, adaptability, adaptability' rather than location alone.
Sarah Johnson of Real Estate Insights Inc. says remote work has created demand for home offices, quiet neighborhoods, and spaces away from traditional economic centers.
City managers and urban planners are tasked with reimagining public spaces, infrastructure and transportation for decentralized communities.
